topic: Day 1 · Variceal Bleeding I — Portal Hypertension & First-Line Control
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Liver Unit & Portal Hypertension Service
speakerBio: A hepatologist who runs the acute liver bleed service. She teaches variceal haemorrhage as a pressure problem first and a clotting problem never — squeeze, shield, and band.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start

A 54-year-old man with known alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought in vomiting large volumes of dark red blood with clots. He is jaundiced, has a distended abdomen, tremulous hands, BP 88/50, HR 124. The registrar reaches for blood and starts transfusing hard. Within twenty minutes he vomits again — more than before. This session is about why the cirrhotic bleed is a different, deadlier animal than the ulcer, and the first-line bundle that saves lives before the endoscope even arrives.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

A variceal bleed is a plumbing problem, not a clotting problem — the pressure in the portal system is too high, and until you drop that pressure and defend against infection, no amount of blood product will hold.

2 · Portal hypertension — the mechanism 🩸

Portal pressure is governed by Ohm's law applied to flow: Pressure = Flow × Resistance. In cirrhosis both terms rise:

  • Increased intrahepatic resistance — the primary event. Fibrosis and regenerative nodules mechanically distort the sinusoids, and there is a dynamic component: a deficiency of intrahepatic nitric oxide leaves the hepatic vascular bed constricted.
  • Increased splanchnic inflow — the amplifier. Portal hypertension triggers splanchnic vasodilation (excess NO in the splanchnic bed, paradoxically), increasing blood flow into an already obstructed portal system. This is why the system spirals.

Blood forced to find a way around the liver decompresses through portosystemic collaterals — the gastro-oesophageal junction being the most dangerous, forming submucosal varices that bulge into the lumen under high pressure with only thin mucosa between them and the world.

🎯 HVPG — measuring the pressure that matters

The hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) = wedged (occluded) hepatic venous pressure − free hepatic venous pressure. It is the clinical surrogate for portal pressure. Thresholds to memorise:

• Normal: 1–5 mmHg. • >5 mmHg: portal hypertension exists. • ≥10 mmHg: clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) — the threshold above which varices form and decompensation begins. • ≥12 mmHg: the threshold below which variceal bleeding essentially does not occur — and the target of pressure-lowering therapy. • >16–20 mmHg: markedly worse prognosis and higher failure of first-line control.

3 · Why the cirrhotic bleed is deadlier ⚠️

Compared with the ulcer patient, the cirrhotic arrives with the deck stacked against them:

  • Coagulopathy — but a rebalanced one. Reduced synthesis of clotting factors and anticoagulants; thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism. The INR does not reflect true bleeding risk and should not be 'corrected' with FFP (which just raises portal pressure — see below).
  • Infection drives rebleeding. Bacterial translocation and endotoxaemia worsen portal pressure and impair the clot; up to ~20% of cirrhotics with a GI bleed are already infected on admission and many more become so. Infection is an independent predictor of failure to control bleeding and death — hence prophylactic antibiotics are core, not optional.
  • Portal-pressure surges from over-transfusion. Pouring in blood and FFP raises portal pressure and precipitates rebleeding — the single most important iatrogenic trap in this disease.
  • Underlying decompensation — hepatic encephalopathy (blood is a protein meal for the gut), renal dysfunction/hepatorenal, and poor reserve mean small insults cascade.
⚠️ Danger — transfusion is a drug with a therapeutic window

The landmark Villanueva trial (NEJM 2013) randomised acute UGIB to a restrictive (transfuse at Hb < 70, target 70–90) versus liberal (transfuse at < 90) strategy. Restrictive transfusion improved 6-week survival — and the benefit was greatest in the Child–Pugh A/B cirrhotics, in whom liberal transfusion caused portal-pressure rises and more rebleeding. The rule: in variceal bleeding, transfuse conservatively to a target of ~70 g/L. More blood is not more safety.

4 · The first-line bundle — three simultaneous moves 🎯

Before and around the endoscopy, three interventions run in parallel. All three have mortality evidence.

PillarAgent / actionWhy it works
1. Vasoactive drugTerlipressin (2 mg IV 4-hourly, titrate down) or octreotide (50 µg bolus + 50 µg/h) — start on suspicion, before endoscopy, continue 2–5 daysSplanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal inflow → ↓ portal pressure and variceal flow. Improves control and reduces mortality.
2. Prophylactic antibioticsCeftriaxone 1 g IV daily (preferred in advanced cirrhosis / high fluoroquinolone-resistance settings), for up to 7 daysPrevents/treats bacterial infection that drives rebleeding and death. Reduces mortality — one of the strongest recommendations in Baveno VII.
3. Endoscopic band ligationEVL within 12 hours of presentation, after resuscitation and vasoactive drugMechanical obliteration of the varix; definitive local haemostasis.
💡 Memory hook — the cirrhotic bleed trio

"Squeeze, shield, band." Squeeze the splanchnic circulation (terlipressin/octreotide), shield against infection (ceftriaxone), band the varix (EVL). Two of the three (drug, antibiotic) are started before the scope, on clinical suspicion alone.

5 · Vasoactive drugs in detail 💊

  • Terlipressin — a vasopressin analogue; longer-acting, given as boluses. Watch for hyponatraemia (can be profound and rapid), ischaemia (mesenteric/cardiac/peripheral) and fluid overload. Avoid in ischaemic heart/peripheral vascular disease.
  • Octreotide / somatostatin — somatostatin analogues; continuous infusion; fewer ischaemic effects, favoured where terlipressin is contraindicated.
  • All reduce portal pressure by splanchnic vasoconstriction; started on suspicion (even before diagnostic endoscopy) and continued 2–5 days to cover the high-risk early rebleed window.

6 · Why banding beats sclerotherapy 🎯

Endoscopic variceal band ligation (EVL) has replaced injection sclerotherapy for oesophageal varices. A rubber band is deployed over an aspirated varix, strangulating it; it thromboses and sloughs, leaving a healed scar.

Band ligation (EVL)Sclerotherapy
MechanismMechanical strangulation of the varixChemical injection → inflammation/thrombosis
RebleedingLowerHigher
ComplicationsFewer; shallow ulcersDeep ulcers, strictures, perforation, mediastinitis, bacteraemia
EradicationFewer sessionsMore sessions
StatusFirst-line for oesophageal varicesLargely abandoned; niche rescue only

Sclerotherapy survives only where banding is technically impossible or as a rescue. For gastric varices the calculus differs (glue/cyanoacrylate) — that is Session 7's territory.

7 · Baveno VII — the definitions that structure everything 📖

Baveno VII (2022) is the consensus that governs modern variceal care. Key definitions:

  • Clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH): HVPG ≥ 10 mmHg (or non-invasive surrogates: liver stiffness ≥ 25 kPa; or ≥ 20 kPa + platelets < 150 = the 'Baveno VI/VII' rule-in criteria).
  • Acute variceal bleeding time-frame: the episode spans the 120 hours (5 days) from presentation — the window of highest rebleed risk.
  • Failure to control bleeding (within 5 days): fresh haematemesis / NG aspirate of ≥ 100 mL ≥ 2 h after starting drug or endoscopic therapy; development of hypovolaemic shock; or a 3 g/dL Hb drop (~9% haematocrit) within 24 h without transfusion. This defines the patient who has failed first-line and needs rescue (Session 7).
  • Timing of endoscopy: within 12 hours of presentation for acute variceal bleeding.
🎯 Concept — 'decompensation' vs 'further decompensation'

Baveno VII reframes cirrhosis by stage. Variceal bleeding is a decompensating event; a patient who has already bled and then develops ascites or encephalopathy has undergone further decompensation, which carries a far worse prognosis. This staging is why we treat the first bleed so aggressively and think early about definitive pressure-lowering (pre-emptive TIPS — Session 7).

8 · Putting it together — the first hour of a variceal bleed ⏱️

  1. Airway first. Massive haematemesis + encephalopathy = high aspiration risk; have a low threshold for intubation to protect the airway before endoscopy.
  2. Resuscitate restrictively. Crossmatch; transfuse to Hb ~70. Do not blindly correct INR with FFP; give platelets/fibrinogen per specialist guidance if markedly deranged and bleeding.
  3. Start terlipressin (or octreotide) immediately on suspicion.
  4. Give ceftriaxone 1 g IV.
  5. Endoscopy within 12 h → band ligation of oesophageal varices.
  6. Consider early/pre-emptive TIPS in the highest-risk (Session 7). Start lactulose for encephalopathy prophylaxis (blood in gut).
☠️ M&M — "We chased the numbers"

A 58-year-old woman with Child–Pugh B cirrhosis presented with a moderate variceal bleed, BP 100/60, Hb 78. Anxious about the cirrhosis, the covering team transfused 4 units of red cells and 2 of FFP to 'get the Hb up and fix the clotting,' pushing her Hb to 112. Terlipressin was started late and ceftriaxone was forgotten in the rush. Ninety minutes later she had a torrential rebleed and became haemodynamically unstable; she developed a spontaneous bacterial peritonitis two days on. Errors: (1) over-transfusion raised her portal pressure and precipitated the rebleed — the Villanueva restrictive target of ~70 was ignored; (2) FFP to 'correct' the INR added volume and portal pressure without fixing a rebalanced haemostatic system; (3) omitted prophylactic antibiotic, one of the few interventions with a clear mortality benefit. Lesson: in variceal bleeding you win by lowering portal pressure and preventing infection — not by maximising the haemoglobin. Restrict the transfusion, start the drug and the antibiotic early, and leave the INR alone.

9 · Take-home wiring diagram

  • Mechanism: ↑ intrahepatic resistance and ↑ splanchnic inflow → portal hypertension → collateral varices. HVPG ≥ 10 = varices form; ≥ 12 = bleeding possible and the treatment target.
  • Deadlier because: rebalanced coagulopathy (don't fix the INR), infection drives rebleeding, and over-transfusion surges portal pressure.
  • Transfuse restrictively to Hb ~70 (Villanueva) — most benefit in cirrhotics.
  • First-line bundle = squeeze, shield, band: terlipressin/octreotide + ceftriaxone 1 g + EVL within 12 h. Drug and antibiotic start on suspicion.
  • Band, not sclerotherapy — lower rebleeding and fewer complications.
  • Baveno VII: defines CSPH, the 5-day acute window, and failure-to-control criteria (rebleed / shock / 3 g Hb drop) — the trigger for rescue therapy.

Next session: what to do when this bundle fails — balloon tamponade, oesophageal stents, and the pre-emptive TIPS that can rewrite survival.

moderatorQs.q: What are the key HVPG thresholds and why do 10 and 12 mmHg matter so much?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The hepatic venous pressure gradient (wedged minus free hepatic venous pressure) is the clinical surrogate for portal pressure; normal is 1–5 mmHg. Above 5 mmHg portal hypertension exists, but the two thresholds that drive management are: ≥ 10 mmHg = clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH), the level above which varices form and clinical decompensation (bleeding, ascites) becomes possible; and ≥ 12 mmHg, below which variceal bleeding essentially does not occur — making 12 the physiological target of pressure-lowering therapy (non-selective beta-blockers, TIPS). A gradient reduced below 12, or by ≥ 10–20% from baseline, markedly lowers bleeding risk. An HVPG above ~16–20 identifies patients at high risk of failing first-line control.

moderatorQs.q: Why is prophylactic antibiotic therapy considered a mortality-reducing intervention in variceal bleeding, not merely supportive care?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because in cirrhosis, bacterial infection is causally linked to failure to control bleeding and to death, not just an incidental complication. Bacterial translocation and endotoxaemia raise portal pressure and impair haemostasis, directly promoting rebleeding; a large proportion of cirrhotics are infected on admission or become so. Randomised trials and meta-analyses show that prophylactic antibiotics reduce infections, rebleeding AND mortality — one of the strongest recommendations in Baveno VII. The preferred agent in advanced cirrhosis or high-resistance settings is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily for up to 7 days. It is given to every cirrhotic with GI bleeding, started at presentation regardless of whether infection is yet apparent.

moderatorQs.q: A registrar wants to transfuse a Child–Pugh B variceal bleeder aggressively and correct the INR with FFP. Why is this dangerous?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Both moves can precipitate rebleeding. The Villanueva trial (NEJM 2013) showed a restrictive transfusion strategy (target Hb ~70 g/L) improved 6-week survival versus a liberal one, with the greatest benefit in Child–Pugh A/B cirrhotics — because pouring in volume raises portal pressure and blows the fragile clot. FFP to 'correct' the INR is doubly wrong: the elevated INR does not reflect true bleeding risk in cirrhosis (haemostasis is rebalanced — both pro- and anticoagulant factors fall), so FFP corrects a number rather than a physiological deficit, while adding volume that further raises portal pressure. The correct approach is restrictive transfusion to ~70, leave the INR alone, and lower portal pressure pharmacologically with terlipressin or octreotide.

audienceQs.q: When should I intubate a variceal bleeder before endoscopy rather than proceed with sedation alone?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Have a low threshold to intubate for airway protection whenever there is massive ongoing haematemesis, altered consciousness or hepatic encephalopathy — the combination that makes aspiration of blood highly likely and often lethal. Active large-volume bleeding fills the pharynx faster than suction can clear it, and an encephalopathic patient cannot protect their own airway. Elective pre-endoscopic intubation gives a controlled airway, allows safe sedation for a technically demanding therapeutic scope, and prevents aspiration pneumonia which independently worsens outcome. In a fully alert patient with a modest, controlled bleed you may proceed with careful conscious sedation, but the moment consciousness is impaired or bleeding is torrential, secure the airway first.

audienceQs.q: What do I watch for on terlipressin, and when would octreotide be preferred instead?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Terlipressin is a vasopressin analogue, so its adverse effects are vasoconstrictive and osmotic: watch for ischaemia (myocardial, mesenteric, peripheral/digital, cerebral), hyponatraemia (which can be rapid and severe — monitor sodium closely, especially in younger patients with preserved liver function), fluid retention and bradycardia. Avoid or use with great caution in ischaemic heart disease, significant peripheral vascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension. In those patients, or if ischaemic complications develop, switch to octreotide/somatostatin (a somatostatin analogue given as a 50 µg bolus then 50 µg/h infusion), which lowers portal pressure with a much lower ischaemic burden. Either agent is continued for 2–5 days to cover the high-risk rebleed window.

audienceQs.q: Why has band ligation replaced sclerotherapy for oesophageal varices?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because endoscopic variceal band ligation (EVL) is both safer and more effective. EVL strangulates the varix mechanically with a rubber band, causing it to thrombose and slough with a shallow, healing ulcer. Sclerotherapy injects a chemical irritant, causing deeper tissue injury. Head-to-head, banding gives lower rebleeding rates, fewer complications (sclerotherapy causes deep ulcers, oesophageal strictures, perforation, mediastinitis and bacteraemia) and eradicates varices in fewer sessions. It is therefore first-line for oesophageal varices, and sclerotherapy is reserved for the rare situation where banding is technically impossible. Note this applies to oesophageal varices — gastric varices are treated differently, with cyanoacrylate glue.
